Use the information in the table to complete the network diagram where the edges are labelled with distances.

\exfigure{300_q17_1}

Mahsa wants to travel from Hobart to Darwin. She wants to change planes only once.

Using the network diagram, calculate how many kilometres she will travel by plane.

criteria: Provides a diagram that is substantially correct, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Solution is the completed network diagram, already referenced by \exfigure{300_q17_s1}.

solutions.latex:
Using the network diagram, the route with one change of plane is Hobart to the intermediate city, then to Darwin.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Kilometres travelled} &= 1040 + 3150 \\ &= 4190 \text{ km}\end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: option B: hexagon with three diagonals

parts.latex:
Team $A$ and Team $B$ have entered a chess competition.

Team $A$ and Team $B$ have three members each. Each member of Team $A$ must play each member of Team $B$ once.

Which of the following network diagrams could represent the chess games to be played?

solutions.latex:
Each of the 3 members of Team $A$ plays each of the 3 members of Team $B$ once, so there are $3\times 3 = 9$ games, and so 9 edges.

No one plays a team-mate, so every edge joins a member of $A$ to a member of $B$.

Count the edges in each diagram:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{A} &: 6 \text{ edges} \\ \text{B} &: 6 + 3 = 9 \text{ edges} \\ \text{C} &: 12 \text{ edges} \\ \text{D} &: 15 \text{ edges} \end{aligned}$$
Only diagram B has 9 edges.

In B, label the vertices $1$ to $6$ around the hexagon, and let Team $A$ be the odd vertices and Team $B$ the even vertices. The hexagon sides and the three long diagonals each join an odd vertex to an even vertex, and each odd vertex is joined to all three even vertices.
$$\therefore\ \text{Diagram B}$$

meta.self_check: Edge counts read from the figure crops: A hexagon only (6), B hexagon plus 3 long diagonals (9, forms K3,3), C hexagon plus all 6 short diagonals (12), D complete graph (15).

parts.latex:
What is the sum of the degrees of the vertices in the network shown below?

\exfigure{722_q4_1}

solutions.latex:
The sum of the degrees of the vertices is twice the number of edges (each edge contributes to two vertices).

The network has $6$ edges, so the sum is
$$2\times 6 = 12$$
This is option D.

figures.cap: network with vertices A to E

solutions.latex:
The degree of a vertex is the number of edge ends at it (the double edge $AB$ counts twice).
$$\begin{aligned} \deg A &= 4 \ (AB,AB,AC,AE)\\ \deg B &= 3 \ (AB,AB,BC)\\ \deg C &= 4 \ (AC,BC,CD,CE)\\ \deg D &= 2 \ (CD,DE)\\ \deg E &= 3 \ (AE,CE,DE) \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Sum} = 4+3+4+2+3 = 16$$
Check: there are $8$ edges and the sum of the degrees is twice the number of edges, $2\times 8 = 16$. The answer is D.

parts.latex:
The map shows regions within a country.

\exfigure{40_q4_1}

A network diagram is to be drawn to represent this map. Vertices will be used to indicate each region and edges will be used to represent a border shared between two regions.

How many edges will there be in the network diagram?

solutions.latex:
Each shared border is one edge. Listing the borders between pairs of regions:
$$\begin{aligned} &\text{Forest–Swamp},\ \text{Forest–Mountains},\ \text{Swamp–Mountains},\\ &\text{Mountains–Desert},\ \text{Mountains–Woods},\ \text{Woods–Desert},\ \text{Desert–Coast} \end{aligned}$$
There are $7$ borders, so the network diagram has $7$ edges.

Hence the answer is B.

meta.self_check: Counted borders from the map; Swamp and Desert only meet at a point on the outer boundary and Coast touches only Desert, so neither adds an edge.

40_q4_1.notes: Map of six regions (Forest, Swamp, Mountains, Desert, Coast, Woods), each with a filled triangle marker. The internal borders match closely, and so do the adjacencies (the 7 shared borders the question counts). The wiggly outer coastline is only an approximation, drawn as smooth splines through traced points: the narrow inlets on the Woods/Forest coast are less deep than in the crop. That accounts for most of the low overlay score. Region names are slightly larger than in the print. Upright text is kept because these are place names, not maths.
